snippet.title: Why is getting bitten by a rabid animal so dangerous? - Charles Rupprecht
snippet.description:
Take a look at what makes rabies the most lethal infectious disease, and what measures you should take if you're exposed to it.

--

In 1885, Joseph Meister was bit in 14 places by a rabid dog. His mother rushed him to Paris for an experimental vaccine from Louis Pasteur, and he became the first rabies-vaccinated person to survive. Today, without proper intervention, rabies remains deadly in almost all cases. So, what makes it so dangerous to humans? Charles Rupprecht explores what makes this infectious disease so lethal.

snippet.title: 52 Americans Held Hostage for 444 Days And Released at Reagan Inauguration #history #facts
snippet.description:
On November 4, 1979, Iranian militants stormed the US Embassy in Tehran and took 66 Americans hostage. They were blindfolded, beaten, paraded on live television, and subjected to mock executions. A US rescue attempt failed, killing 8 American servicemen in the desert. 52 hostages were held for 444 days. They were released the exact minute Ronald Reagan was sworn in as president on January 20, 1981.

snippet.title: Information Systems Explained | How Businesses Use Data and Technology
snippet.description:
Modern organisations depend on information.

They need information about:
Customers.
Employees.
Sales.
Stock.
Finances.
Operations.
But collecting data is not enough.
Businesses need systems that can organise that data and turn it into useful information.

Here’s the reality:
An Information System is an organised combination of people, technology, data, and processes used to collect, process, store, and distribute information.
In this lecture, we explain Information Systems and examine how organisations use them to operate efficiently and make better decisions.

What You’ll Learn
• what an Information System actually is
• the main components of an Information System
• how data becomes useful information
• how businesses use Information Systems
• why people and processes matter as much as technology

Core Concepts
• people
• hardware
• software
• data
• processes
• networks
• information

Main Components of an Information System
• People – employees, managers, customers, and technical specialists
• Hardware – computers, servers, scanners, and other physical devices
• Software – applications and programs that process information
• Data – facts and records collected by the organisation
• Processes – rules and steps explaining how the system is used
• Networks – connections that allow devices and people to exchange information

Real-World Examples
• supermarket checkout systems
• hospital patient-record systems
• university student portals
• banking applications
• restaurant ordering systems
• online shopping platforms
• employee-management systems

The Real Shift
• from computers → complete organisational systems
• from raw data → useful information
• from isolated departments → connected operations
• from guessing → evidence-based decisions

Reality Check
• an Information System is not just software
• technology cannot fix a badly designed process
• inaccurate data produces unreliable information
• employees must understand how to use the system
• cybersecurity and privacy are essential

Why This Matters
Without effective Information Systems:
• employees may waste time finding information
• departments may become disconnected
• customers may receive poor service
• managers may make decisions using inaccurate data
• businesses may lose money and opportunities

Because at the end:
Information Systems are not simply about computers — they are about connecting people, data, technology, and processes to help organisations work smarter.

snippet.title: Bureaucracy Explained | How Government Organisations Work
snippet.description:
Bureaucracy is a system used to organise governments and large institutions through rules, hierarchy, specialised jobs, and formal procedures.

In this video, we explain how bureaucracy works, why governments use it, its main features, and how excessive bureaucracy can create red tape and slow decision-making.

What You’ll Learn
• what bureaucracy means
• why governments use bureaucratic systems
• the main features of bureaucracy
• its advantages and disadvantages
• how red tape develops

What Is Bureaucracy?
Bureaucracy is an organisational system based on:
• clear authority
• written rules
• specialised roles
• formal procedures
• professional officials
• levels of management
Each employee has defined responsibilities.
Decisions are made through official processes rather than personal preference.

Main Features
Max Weber explained bureaucracy through several key features:
• hierarchy
• division of labour
• written rules
• merit-based recruitment
• professional officials
• impersonal decisions
These features help organisations remain stable and predictable.

Why Governments Use Bureaucracy
Governments manage millions of people and many public services.
Bureaucracy helps them:
• divide responsibilities
• maintain records
• apply laws consistently
• manage public money
• coordinate departments
• hold officials accountable
Without formal systems, decisions could become disorganised or unfair.

Simple Example
Imagine someone applies for a driving licence.
The application follows a formal process:
• identity is verified
• documents are checked
• fees are paid
• rules are applied
• the licence is approved or rejected
The decision should be based on official requirements, not personal connections.
That is bureaucracy in practice.
Advantages of Bureaucracy

Bureaucracy can provide:
• consistency
• accountability
• clear responsibilities
• professional management
• equal procedures
• organisational stability
Written rules can reduce favouritism and personal bias.

Disadvantages of Bureaucracy
Too much bureaucracy can create:
• slow decisions
• unnecessary paperwork
• rigid rules
• poor customer service
• weak innovation
• repeated approvals
• red tape
When officials focus more on procedures than outcomes, the system becomes inefficient.

Reality Check
Bureaucracy is not automatically bad.
Large governments need rules, departments, and clear responsibilities.
The real problem begins when procedures become more important than the people they are supposed to serve.

And here is the brutal truth:
Rules should support public service, not become obstacles to it.
Why This Matters
Understanding bureaucracy explains:
• how government departments operate
• why officials follow procedures
• how responsibilities are divided
• why public decisions can be slow
• how red tape affects citizens

Because at the end:
Bureaucracy creates order, but without reform and accountability, it can also create delay and frustration.

snippet.title: Is the US Dollar Losing Power? China’s CIPS Explained
snippet.description:
The global financial system may be changing — and most people don’t even realize it.

China has been quietly building an alternative to the traditional Western banking network like SWIFT. It’s called Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), launched in 2015 by the People's Bank of China.

Originally designed to settle transactions in yuan, CIPS is now expanding to support multiple currencies and cross-border payment channels. This could reduce dependence on the US dollar — which currently dominates global trade and gives the United States major control through financial sanctions.

Countries like Russia and Iran are already exploring alternatives.

So the big question is:
Are we moving toward a multipolar financial system with multiple global payment networks?

Watch till the end to understand what this means for the future of money.

Originally designed to settle transactions in yuan, CIPS is now expanding to support multiple currencies and cross-border payment channels. This could reduce dependence on the US dollar — which currently dominates global trade and gives the United States major control through financial sanctions.

Countries like Russia and Iran are already exploring alternatives.

So the big question is:
Are we moving toward a multipolar financial system with multiple global payment networks?

snippet.title: How do snakes swallow animals so much bigger than they are? - Niko Zlotnik
snippet.description:
Explore how snakes evolved, and find out how their jaw-dropping anatomy allows them to take down prey several times their size.

--

Since slithering onto the scene some 150 million years ago, evolving length and limbless-ness out of their ancestral lizard forms, snakes have diversified rapidly. Their noodly bodies and flexible heads granted them access to novel places and prey. And today, there are nearly 4,000 snake species, spanning habitats high and low. Niko Zlotnik explores how snakes evolved into incredible predators.

Lesson by Niko Zlotnik, directed by Anna Benner.
